Since often a reassessment leads to an action, The first 2 re assessment triggers for any trade are always the stop-loss and take-profit after that, you record. Anything else that might change your mind, the goal for this stage of the process is to try to guess xante, what might be signal and what might be noise going forward. When you have a trade on every price movement, feels like a signal or a sign of danger for your position. While in reality most price movement is noise. every time price Jiggles lower or ratchets higher, you'll have an emotional reaction because you're invested the idea with reassessment triggers is to codify what will make you change your mind and what will not before the price starts flickering and jiggling around, and those dumb voices in your head, start to react to that flickering and jiggling, Some other examples of good reassessment triggers. A long stocks because I think the FED has turned more devish and the market hasn't caught on yet. There are 2 fed speakers this week. If either 1 of those speakers is more hawkish than I expect. If either copper or iron ore break below their 200 hour moving average, I'll reassess my Aussie dollar long position If you take the time to record these reassessment triggers, you should find very few occasions where you make on the fly to decisions made trade. Once you have a trade on, leave it alone and let it bake. Don't rush it, don't keep opening the oven to Peak the market doesn't care about your time frame. A market that is not moving is boring but it's not telling you anything. Wait for your stop-loss your take profit or 1 of your reassessment triggers to hit stop white knuckling. Of course, there are going to be times when you're long and bad news comes out and you hit a bin and you save yourself some cash but these are not all that. Common just, as often, you'll hit the bid and find yourself, buying the stock back, 10 minutes later after realizing the news wasn't, as bad as you thought. And in fact, the news was actually meaningless. Remember that when you have a trade on you are biased. Information processing is distorted by your emotional state. The best action is almost always no action. This is true when you have a position on and it's also true. Most of the time when you don't Let me your actions as much as possible and you will put on only the best trades. Then you'll stay in those trades long enough for them to bear fruit. This Is My Kryptonite and the greatest strengths and greatest weakness in my life. I can do a thousand push-ups in a day every Wednesday for 10th, straight weeks action but have an incredibly tough time. Going 2 hours with that touching the buyer or sell buttons in action. This bias to action, gives me the energy to write a decent macro newsletter every day, and to pump out a book every year or 2, but it also makes it shockingly difficult for me to sit at work. And keep my hands off the trading controls. My default mode is action. I've known that for 20 years and yet is still my greatest weakness in trading. I never stopped working on it, but I also accept it is who I am. I forgive myself more easily now than I did when I was 30. I try to automate as much as possible and convince myself to sit there and do nothing as much as possible. Once, you know, your personal Kryptonite, fine-tune your process and redesign your framework to address it. 4 position sizing. Position size is a function of 6 factors 1 convention level 2 free Capital 3 year to date, pno 4, Market volatility, 5, distance, from entry point to stop-loss and 6, Gap and liquidity risk. Here's a quick summary of how to determine position size. A toad on your conviction level. B given your year to date, p&l and free capital. Decide on a percentage of your Capital to put at risk. This tells you how many dollars or basis points, you'll be risking on the trade C, using Market volatility and technical analysis. Choose the appropriate stop-loss D. Calculate the position size, which is dollars at risk, divided by risk per unit to get the total number of units. E, think about liquidity, is this a reasonable position size? Can you get in and out with that much of an issue? If not, can you scale in and out and maintain the economics of the trade? And F think about Gap risks. What major events are coming up, how is the product been trading? Do you need to worry about limit up and limit down? Is there enough liquidity for this position size? In this step? You might reduce your position size because of a gap risk or consider exiting the trade before an upcoming event. I'll go through this process again in the trade.
